questions.question: .  Cadaveric anatomy is studied on:
options:
All
 Correct: [B].  Cadaveric anatomy deals with macroscopic structural dissection performed on preserved human corpses (cadavers).
Microscopic study is histology; models and virtual bodies represent prosections or synthetic simulators.

questions.question: .  Living anatomy includes:
options:
Endoscopy
 E) All  ✓
 Correct: [E].  Living anatomy is investigated in vivo through physical examination techniques (inspection, palpation, percussion,
auscultation) and modern clinical adjuncts including plain radiography, ultrasonography, and endoscopic visualization.

questions.question: .  The study of bones and deeper organs by plain/contrast radiography, ultrasound, and CT scan is:
options:
Applied anatomy
E) Surface anatomy
 Correct: [B].  Radiographic (imaging) anatomy utilizes diagnostic electromagnetic radiation, sound waves (USG), and tomography to
delineate deep skeletal and visceral architecture in real time.

questions.question: .  The study of factors that in fl uence and determine the form, structure, and function of different parts of the body is:
options:
Applied anatomy
E) Surface anatomy
 Correct: [A].  Environmental anatomy investigates how extrinsic factors (altitude, climate, mechanical stress, ecological niches)
modify biological form and function.

questions.question: .  The study dealing with external features and measurements of different human races and groups is:
options:
Physical anthropology  ✓
 E) Surface anatomy
 Correct: [D].  Physical (biological) anthropology evaluates anthropometric variations, craniometry, racial characteristics, and
evolutionary adaptation across human populations.

questions.question: .  The study of deeper parts of the body in relation to the skin surface is:
options:
Physical anthropology
 E) Surface anatomy  ✓
 Correct: [E].  Surface (topographical) anatomy uses palpable and visible surface landmarks to project the precise location and
boundaries of deeper neurovascular structures and viscera.
 PART 2: HISTORICAL FIGURES & FOUNDATIONAL MILESTONES

questions.question: .  Father of Medicine is:
options:
None
 Correct: [A].  Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460 – 370 BC) established clinical ethics (Hippocratic Oath) and separated medicine from
superstition, earning him the title Father of Medicine.
 Chapter 01: Introduction to General Anatomy  Page 1 of 4

PART 2 CONTINUED: HISTORICAL FIGURES & FOUNDATIONAL MILESTONES

questions.question: .  Father of Anatomy is:
options:
None
 Correct: [B].  Herophilus of Chalcedon (335 – 280 BC), alongside Erasistratus, was the  fi rst to systematically dissect human
cadavers publicly at Alexandria, earning him the title Father of Anatomy. (Andreas Vesalius is recognized as Father of Modern
Anatomy).

questions.question: .  Prince of Physicians is:
options:
Galen  ✓
 Correct: [D].  Claudius Galenus (Galen of Pergamon, 129 – c. 216 AD) was designated the "Prince of Physicians"; his extensive
anatomical and humoral doctrines dominated Western medical thought for over 1,300 years.

questions.question: .  The originator of cross-sectional anatomy is:
options:
None
 Correct: [C].  Leonardo da Vinci (1452 – 1519) pioneered transverse section drawings and multi-angle views of organs and
musculoskeletal systems, laying the groundwork for modern sectional imaging.

questions.question: .  Who discovered the circulation of blood?
options:
William Harvey  ✓
 Correct: [D].  English physician William Harvey published *Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus* in
1628, demonstrating that blood circulates continuously through a closed systemic loop driven by the heart.
 PART 3: FUNDAMENTAL ANATOMICAL POSITIONS

questions.question:
.  When a person is lying on her/his back, arms by the side, palms facing upwards, and feet put together, the position
is:
options:
Lithotomical position
 Correct: [A].  The supine position denotes dorsal recumbency with the ventral surface facing upward towards the ceiling.

questions.question: .  A person lying on his/her face, chest, and abdomen is said to be in:
options:
Lithotomical position
 Correct: [B].  The prone position designates ventral recumbency, with the dorsum directed superiorly and anterior trunk resting on
the surface.
 Chapter 01: Introduction to General Anatomy  Page 2 of 4

PART 3 CONTINUED: ANATOMICAL POSITIONS & SECTIONAL PLANES

questions.question: .  Person lying on her back with legs up and feet supported in straps. This position is:
options:
Lithotomical position  ✓
 Correct: [D].  The lithotomy position features a supine patient with hips and knees  fl exed, thighs abducted, and calves/feet elevated
in stirrups. It is the clinical standard for pelvic exams, childbirth, and perineal surgeries.

questions.question:
.  When a person is standing straight with eyes looking forwards, both arms by the side of body, palms facing
forwards, both feet together, the position is:
options:
Lithotomical position
 Correct: [C].  The standard anatomical position is the universal baseline reference for all directional terminology, de fi ned by erect
standing, forward gaze, arms at sides, palms directed anteriorly, and heels together.

questions.question: .  A plane parallel to the median or midsagittal plane is the:
options:
Transverse plane
 Correct: [A].  While the median (midsagittal) plane is singular and centered, any vertical slice oriented parallel to it is termed a
sagittal (or parasagittal) plane, dividing the structure into unequal right and left parts.

questions.question: .  A plane passing through the centre of the body dividing it into two equal halves (right and left) is:
options:
Transverse plane
 E) B and C  ✓
 Correct: [E].  Both "Median plane" and "Midsagittal plane" refer synonymously to the midline longitudinal plane dividing the body into
symmetrical right and left halves.

questions.question: .  A plane at right angles to the sagittal/median plane which divides the body into anterior and posterior parts is:
options:
Transverse plane
 E) Coronal plane  ✓
 Correct: [E].  The coronal (frontal) plane runs vertically from side to side perpendicular to the median axis, cleaving the body into
front (anterior/ventral) and back (posterior/dorsal) sections.

questions.question:
.  A plane at right angles to both sagittal and coronal planes which divides the body into upper and lower parts is
called:
options:
Transverse plane  ✓
 E) Coronal plane
 Correct: [D].  The transverse (horizontal or axial) plane cuts horizontally across the longitudinal axis, separating superior (cranial)
segments from inferior (caudal) segments.
 Chapter 01: Introduction to General Anatomy  Page 3 of 4

PART 4: JOINT MOVEMENTS & GENERAL TERMINOLOGY / PATHOLOGY

questions.question: .  In which of the following movements does the angle between articulating surfaces NOT change?
options:
Extension
 Correct: [B].  Gliding movements (typical of planar synovial joints like intercarpal/intertarsal joints) involve  fl at bone surfaces sliding
past one another without angular deviation or rotary movement.

questions.question: .  When the tip of the thumb touches the tip of any of the  fi ngers, it is:
options:
Flexion
 Correct: [A].  Opposition is a composite movement facilitated by the 1st carpometacarpal saddle joint ( fl exion, abduction, medial
rotation) bringing the palmar aspect of the thumb pad against another digital pad.

questions.question: .  The precapillary or postcapillary communication between vessels is called:
options:
Aponeurosis
 Correct: [A].  An anastomosis is a direct intervascular junction connecting adjacent arterioles, venules, or capillary channels,
providing alternate collateral pathways for blood  fl ow.

questions.question: .  A form of necrosis (tissue death) combined with putrefaction is:
options:
None
 Correct: [A].  Gangrene represents macroscopic tissue death caused by ischemia that is subsequently superimposed with bacterial
decay, saprophytic decomposition, and liquefactive putrefaction.

questions.question: .  Increase in tissue/organ size due to an increase in the NUMBER of cells is:
options:
Aplasia
 Correct: [A].  Hyperplasia denotes organ enlargement driven by mitotic cell proliferation (increased cell count), common in labile or
stable cell populations under hormonal or compensatory stress.

questions.question: .  Increase in the size of an organ/tissue without any increase in the number of cells is:
options:
Aplasia
 Correct: [B].  Hypertrophy is cell enlargement resulting from increased synthesis of structural proteins and intracellular organelles
(e.g., skeletal or cardiac muscle  fi bers), not cellular division.
 Quick Revision Matrix (Cellular Adaptations):
 Hypertrophy:  ↑  Cell Size  Hyperplasia:  ↑  Cell Number  Atrophy:  ↓  Cell Size/Mass  Aplasia:  Failure to develop
 Chapter 01: Introduction to General Anatomy  Page 4 of 4

chapters.title: Upper Limb
chapters.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
.  A 24-year-old motorcyclist is thrown from his bike, landing violently on his shoulder while his
head is forced to the opposite side. Examination reveals an adducted, internally rotated arm
with an extended elbow and pronated forearm ("waiter's tip" posture). Which roots of the
brachial plexus are most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
This presentation describes  Erb-Duchenne palsy (Erb's palsy) , caused by traction or rupture of
the upper trunk (roots C5 and C6) due to an excessive increase in the angle between neck and shoulder.
Damage to the suprascapular, axillary, and musculocutaneous nerves paralyzes the abductors (deltoid,
supraspinatus), lateral rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor), elbow flexors (biceps, brachialis), and supinators
(biceps brachii), producing the classic "waiter's tip" limb posture.
 SHOULDER & ROTATOR CUFF

questions.question:
.  A 52-year-old painter reports severe pain when abducting the right arm, especially between 60°
and 120°. On examination, he is completely unable to initiate the first 15° of abduction. Which
muscle is most likely torn?
questions.explanation:
The  supraspinatus  muscle (innervated by the suprascapular nerve, C5–C6) initiates the first 0°–
15° of arm abduction at the glenohumeral joint. The deltoid muscle continues abduction from 15° to 90°, while
the trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the scapula upwards beyond 90°. Supraspinatus is the most
commonly torn rotator cuff tendon due to subacromial impingement.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 1 of 7

HUMERUS FRACTURES & PERIPHERAL NERVES

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
.  A mid-shaft fracture of the humerus is most likely to injure which nerve and associated blood
vessel located along the radial (spiral) groove?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
questions.answer: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
questions.explanation:
The  radial nerve  and  profunda brachii artery  (deep artery of the arm) course together along the
spiral groove on the posterior surface of the humeral shaft. Mid-shaft fractures frequently lacerate or entrap the
radial nerve, leading to "wrist drop" (loss of wrist and finger extension) and sensory loss on the dorsum of the
first web space.
 WRIST & HAND ANATOMY

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
.  A 45-year-old computer programmer presents with nocturnal tingling, numbness, and burning
pain over the palmar aspect of the lateral three and a half digits. Thenar muscle wasting is
noted. Which structure is spared because its branch does not pass through the carpal tunnel?
options: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
questions.answer: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
questions.explanation:
In  carpal tunnel syndrome , structures traversing deep to the flexor retinaculum (median nerve, 4
FDS tendons, 4 FDP tendons, 1 FPL tendon) are compressed. However, the  palmar cutaneous branch  of the
median nerve branches off approximately 5 cm proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes  superficial  to it,
preserving cutaneous sensation over the central palm.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 2 of 7

CARPAL BONES & CLINICAL PATHOLOGY

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
.  Following a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH), a 21-year-old athlete has tenderness in the
anatomical snuffbox. Radiographs confirm a fracture across the waist of the scaphoid. What is
the most significant clinical risk associated with this fracture?
options: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
questions.answer: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
questions.explanation:
The blood supply to the  scaphoid bone  is retrograde, entering primarily via distal branches of the
radial artery and flowing from distal to proximal. A fracture across the scaphoid waist interrupts blood flow to the
proximal segment, predisposing it to nonunion and  avascular necrosis (AVN) .
 ANATOMICAL SPACES

questions.question:
.  Which structure traverses the quadrangular space of the posterior scapular region alongside
the axillary nerve?
questions.explanation:
The  quadrangular space  is bounded superiorly by teres minor (or subscapularis), inferiorly by
teres major, medially by the long head of triceps brachii, and laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus. It
transmits the  axillary nerve  and  posterior circumflex humeral artery . Fractures of the surgical neck or
anterior shoulder dislocations can compromise both structures.
 CUBITAL FOSSA RELATIONS

questions.question:
.  From medial to lateral, what is the correct anatomical sequence of the deep contents located
within the cubital fossa?
options: Radial nerve → Biceps tendon → Brachial artery → Median nerve
Median nerve → Brachial artery → Biceps brachii tendon → Radial nerve
Brachial artery → Median nerve → Biceps tendon → Radial nerve
Biceps tendon → Brachial artery → Median nerve → Ulnar nerve
questions.answer: Median nerve → Brachial artery → Biceps brachii tendon → Radial nerve
questions.explanation:
From  medial to lateral , the mnemonic  "MBBR"  (Median nerve, Brachial artery, Biceps tendon,
Radial nerve [deep between brachialis and brachioradialis]) outlines the contents. Clinically, the bicipital
aponeurosis separates these deep contents from the superficial median cubital vein, protecting the artery during
venipuncture.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 3 of 7

BRACHIAL PLEXUS & NERVE INJURY

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
.  A difficult breech delivery involving excessive upward traction on the upper limb damages the
lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1). The infant demonstrates a "claw hand" posture and
ipsilateral Horner syndrome. What is this clinical condition called?
questions.explanation:
Klumpke palsy  results from lower trunk (C8–T1) brachial plexus injury, typically due to upward
pulling on an abducted arm (e.g., breech delivery or grabbing a tree branch while falling). It paralyzes intrinsic
hand muscles (lumbricals, interossei, thenar/hypothenar), producing a total claw hand. Concomitant injury to the
T1 sympathetic fibers leads to  Horner syndrome  (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
 AXILLA & CHEST WALL

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
.  During a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, the long thoracic nerve of Bell
is accidentally severed. Which deformity will become apparent upon pushing forward against a
wall?
questions.explanation:
The  long thoracic nerve  (roots C5, C6, C7 — "C5, 6, 7 raise your arms to heaven") courses
along the superficial surface of the  serratus anterior  muscle. Denervation impairs scapular protraction and
upward rotation, causing the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula to project posteriorly ("winged
scapula"), especially when pushing against resistance.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 4 of 7

FOREARM & HAND KINEMATICS

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
. Which pair of muscles is responsible for adducting the fingers toward the axial line of the hand
(third digit) and abducting them away from it, respectively?
options: Flexor digitorum profundus and Extensor digitorum
questions.explanation:
Remember the mnemonic  PAD & DAB :  P almar interossei  AD duct the digits toward the midline
(3rd digit), and  D orsal interossei  AB duct the digits away from the midline. All interossei are innervated by the
deep branch of the  ulnar nerve  (C8, T1).
 SURFACE ANATOMY & SPACES

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
. Which tendon forms the medial boundary of the anatomical snuffbox when viewed in the
anatomical position?
questions.explanation:
The  anatomical snuffbox  is bounded medially (posteriorly) by the tendon of  extensor pollicis
longus (EPL) , which hooks around Lister's tubercle on the radius. The lateral (anterior) boundary is formed by
the tendons of  abductor pollicis longus (APL)  and  extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) . The floor contains the
scaphoid, trapezium, and the radial artery.
 ELBOW PATHOLOGY & NERVES

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
. A 19-year-old sustains a medial epicondyle avulsion fracture of the humerus. Which motor and
sensory deficits are most characteristic of this nerve injury?
options: Loss of pronation and sensory loss over the thenar eminence
Clawing of digits 4 and 5 with sensory loss over the medial 1.5 fingers
Wrist drop with sensory loss over the anatomical snuffbox
Inability to abduct the arm past 15° with deltoid anesthesia
questions.answer: Clawing of digits 4 and 5 with sensory loss over the medial 1.5 fingers
questions.explanation:
The  ulnar nerve  runs immediately behind the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel. Fractures
or direct trauma cause motor loss to flexor carpi ulnaris, medial half of FDP, hypothenar muscles, interossei,
and medial 2 lumbricals, culminating in ulnar claw hand (more pronounced in distal lesions: "ulnar paradox")
and anesthesia of the palmar and dorsal aspects of the medial 1.5 fingers.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 5 of 7

AXILLARY ARTERY BRANCHES

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
. The pectoralis minor muscle divides the axillary artery into three anatomical parts. Which
branch arises from the second part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation:
The rule of branches per part of the axillary artery: Part 1 (proximal to pectoralis minor) has  1
branch : Superior thoracic artery.
Part 2 (deep to pectoralis minor) has  2 branches :  Thoracoacromial artery  and Lateral thoracic artery.
Part 3 (distal to pectoralis minor) has  3 branches : Subscapular artery, Anterior circumflex humeral artery, and
Posterior circumflex humeral artery.
 FOREARM & HAND INNERVATION

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
. A patient is unable to make the "OK" sign; instead, when attempting to pinch index finger to
thumb, the distal phalanges remain flat in an abnormal pad-to-pad pinch. Which nerve is
compressed or damaged?
questions.explanation:
The  anterior interosseous nerve (AIN)  is a pure motor branch of the median nerve supplying 3
deep flexors:  flexor pollicis longus ,  lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus  (digits 2 and 3), and  pronator
quadratus . Inability to flex the DIP joint of the index finger and IP joint of the thumb produces a characteristic
pinch deformity rather than a circular "OK" gesture. No cutaneous sensory loss occurs.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 6 of 7

JOINTS & LIGAMENTS

questions.topic: Upper Limb Anatomy MCQs with Explanations
questions.question:
. A 2-year-old child is lifted abruptly by the wrist by an older sibling. The child cries out and holds
the forearm pronated and slightly flexed, refusing to move it ("nursemaid's elbow"). Which
ligament has subluxated over the radial head?
questions.explanation:
In young children, the head of the radius is relatively small and cone-shaped. Sudden axial
traction on an extended, pronated forearm causes the radial head to slip out from the  annular ligament ,
becoming partially trapped between the radial head and the capitulum of the humerus. Gentle supination with
elbow flexion typically reduces the subluxation.
 Clinical Anatomy: Upper Limb Question Bank  Page 7 of 7

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with nocturnal paresthesia in the lateral three and a half digits. Physical exam reveals thenar wasting. Which anatomical structure is spared because its branch does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
options: Palmar cutaneous branch of median nerve
questions.answer: Palmar cutaneous branch of median nerve
questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to it, sparing sensation over the thenar eminence.

questions.question: A motorcyclist suffers traction injury of the upper trunk (C5-C6) of the brachial plexus (Erb-Duchenne palsy). Which classic limb posture is produced?
options: Adducted, internally rotated arm with pronated forearm (Waiter's tip)
Claw hand with loss of hypothenar eminence
Wrist drop with inability to extend digits
Ape hand deformity with thenar atrophy
questions.answer: Adducted, internally rotated arm with pronated forearm (Waiter's tip)
questions.explanation: Loss of abductors (deltoid, supraspinatus) and lateral rotators produces adduction and internal rotation. Loss of biceps causes forearm pronation.

questions.question: Which tendon of the rotator cuff is most commonly involved in impingement syndrome and degenerative tears?
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus tendon passes directly beneath the rigid coracoacromial arch in a critical hypovascular zone, making it most vulnerable to impingement.
